candidates.quote: I was always embarrassed by the words sacred, glorious, and sacrifice and the expression in vain.
candidates.author: Ernest Hemingway
candidates.speaker: Frederic Henry
candidates.whyThisMonth: It names what large abstract words cost and sends a reader back to the concrete names of real things, which is the month in one sentence.

candidates.quote: Look, your worship, what we see there are not giants but windmills, and what seem to be their arms are the sails that turned by the wind make the millstone go.
candidates.author: Miguel de Cervantes
candidates.speaker: Sancho Panza
candidates.whyThisMonth: Sancho says plainly what is actually standing in the field, and saying that out loud to a man who cannot hear it is the discipline of clear seeing.

candidates.quote: Travel is fatal to prejudice, bigotry and narrow-mindedness, and many of our people need it sorely on these accounts.
candidates.author: Mark Twain
candidates.whyThisMonth: It says why a fixed opinion goes soft once a person has actually looked at somewhere else, and it is cheerful about the cure.

candidates.quote: One cannot think well, love well, sleep well, if one has not dined well.
candidates.author: Virginia Woolf
candidates.whyThisMonth: A plain material fact stated without apology, and a useful thing to be told at six in the morning by someone who refuses to pretend otherwise.

candidates.quote: A classic is a book that has never finished saying what it has to say.
candidates.author: Italo Calvino
candidates.locator: definition 6, in The New York Review of Books, 9 October 1986
candidates.whyThisMonth: It tests a book by what it keeps doing rather than by its reputation, which is a clear-eyed measure a reader can apply this morning.

candidates.quote: I am in fact a Hobbit (in all but size).
candidates.author: J. R. R. Tolkien
candidates.work: The Letters of J. R. R. Tolkien
candidates.locator: letter 213, to Deborah Webster, 25 October 1958 (ed. Humphrey Carpenter, 1981)
candidates.whyThisMonth: A famous man describes himself in ordinary words with nothing added for effect, which is what honest self-description actually sounds like.

candidates.quote: Men may dyen of ymaginacioun, / So depe may impressioun be take.
candidates.author: Geoffrey Chaucer
candidates.locator: The Miller’s Tale, lines 3612 to 3613, The Riverside Chaucer
candidates.speaker: the Miller
candidates.whyThisMonth: Six hundred years early it warns that a picture in the head can take hold deeper than the thing itself, which is why looking twice is worth the trouble.

candidates.quote: Give me books, French wine, fruit, fine weather and a little music played out of doors by somebody I do not know.
candidates.author: John Keats
candidates.whyThisMonth: A man says exactly what he wants and stops there, which is plain speech at its most companionable and a good model for the day’s first sentence.

candidates.quote: Eternity is in love with the productions of time.
candidates.author: William Blake
candidates.work: The Marriage of Heaven and Hell
candidates.locator: Proverbs of Hell, the tenth proverb
candidates.whyThisMonth: It puts the weight on what a day actually produces rather than on the idea of it, in nine words that waste none.
